utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening. I am very sorry that in the interest of trying to assist another Chamber, our start today was delayed. And there is a double reason, not only was there no other courtroom available, but Judge Van den Wyngaert was sitting on the other Chamber as well, so we really couldn't get going until now. We hope that we will be able to conclude the present witness in the course of this next tape because there will have to be a tape break at the end of that which would virtually run us out of time. So it may be possible to finish before 7.00 but at the end of the tape, which we can stretch to about 1 hour, 40. Sir, if I could remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Moore

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with one small topic in relation to the hospital itself. When you went to the hospital on the 20th, did you have lists which included the names of people that you wished to speak to or identify?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other person, including Major Sljivancanin, of having a list?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And throughout your dealings there, presumably you would say that you were unaware of the use of lists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say you did not have a list, that you were unaware of other people having lists, but I'm asking you about when you got there, did you see any people operating from a list?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then what was the purpose of taking the list from Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps misunderstood you. I thought that you asked me whether we had -- or made any such lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll break it into two parts. Did you within the security organ at any time compile lists of individuals who might interest you prior to the hospital evacuation on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did this on the basis of the information that we received through our operational work with the names and the nicknames and we relayed that to our superior security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of persons were on that list or lists?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our intelligence, these were the important persons in the chain of command or, in accordance with the reports that we had received, persons who had committed some criminal offences, either against the JNA or the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that lists were given to yourselves and Nicholas Borsinger of persons who were in the hospital. Did you check those lists to see whether any of the persons whom you wished to speak to or identify were actually included in the Bosanac list?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said that the list that we had received, you could not really call it a list at all. These were just scrolls, and we couldn't use it at all, because things were crossed out and added and it was completely useless. And the list that was received by the representatives of the ICRC from Dr. Bosanac, it was neater, and I think it contained more pages that the one that we had been given. Ours had only one or two pages, and it was completely useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The persons that you -- the list of names that you compiled in the course of your work, the names of individuals who were of interest to you, what did you do to identify those persons in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't do anything to identify them. We didn't even have enough time to do it. The lists that we made in the rear of the security organ were something that we needed for our future work when we conducted interviews with ethnic Serbs who would be able to give us more reliable information about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Therefore, in conclusion of this topic, what list did you use on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any list and there, in fact, was no list apart -- if you're asking me about the 20th, then no, no, I did not have any list, just a list that Vesna Bosanac had provided but that list was not something that we could use, and that's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that you became aware of a foreigner. He was tall, he was blond, in a white coat. I use my own note. You said: "I became angry. She had given Borsinger a list of names." You mentioned that to Sljivancanin. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described it -- I described this representative of the ICRC in those terms, and the reason why I was angry is because I didn't know what was on the list, not because she had given him the list. I was angry because we did not have the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have a note which says: "I had a look at Sljivancanin's list." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You misunderstand me. I looked at the list or, rather, the note that was scrolled on this piece of paper that Sljivancanin had told me he had received from Vesna Bosanac telling me that I should not worry, that this was. For all intents and purposes, the same list that had been provided to the representative of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you get angry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was angry because she gave it behind our back, so to speak, and I didn't know at that time that Sljivancanin had already gotten that and that he didn't tell me at the time that I shouldn't worry. Because when she gave it to this man, I thought this was something that we, ourselves, should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how did you know or how did you realise it was nothing like the list of the names of persons given to the ICRC man?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we couldn't use it and it didn't look like the list that I saw her give the representative of the ICRC, so that was the only reason, and that was quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "foreigner," it can often mean a person who is not wanted in that particular location. Would it be right to say that there was a view that the ICRC and the ECMM had no reason to be there, that this was an internal matter?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Surely not. When I said "foreigner," I meant to say a person whose name I didn't know and who I assumed not to be our citizen. I did not mean an undesirable person, because it was not up to us to decide who was desirable and who was not, especially not when it came to representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now move to another topic. You distinguish order and task, would that be right, by way of military directive?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the security organs, there were no orders like there were in the chain of command. There is only control, not command in the security organs. That's the distinction that I've been trying to draw here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you use the phrase "task" as opposed to "order" to represent that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you are given a task, or a person is given a task, can that person refuse to perform the task without good reason, may I say? Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An active-duty serviceman can refuse to obey an order that is against the interests of the constitutional order or an order that would be tantamount to the commission of a criminal offence that is prosecuted ex officio. All other orders or tasks in terms of command, if you look at units, not at institutions or establishments, this is -- these orders have to be carried out. This is the system that applied in the former JNA, and this is, as far as I know, the system that is valid in all the armies of the world. This is the principle of the singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if a person refuses to perform a task, can there be military consequence, a military consequence against him on that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, failure to obey an order results in certain consequences, depending on the actual problems that were caused by the failure to obey this order, and then the commander, within the chain of command, decides to deal with it himself or to bring this person, had this person brought before a military disciplinary court. And in the security organs, failure to obey an order was viewed in a slightly different way, because I can accept an order and yet be prevented from actually carrying it out for a variety of reasons, because our job was a little bit peculiar and it depended on a number of circumstances that could not be foreseen and which could prevent one from actually carrying out the task. Definitely when one submits the report to the security organ that actually issued the task, this security organ will take all those elements into account and decide whether to give them any weight or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it is correct to say that one of the options available would be a person to be brought before a disciplinary court; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you. Depending on the damage caused by the failure to carry out this order, the commander of the unit decides, together with his colleagues at a meeting, whether to deal with a disciplinary infraction himself or whether it has affected the combat readiness of the unit to such an extent that disciplinary proceedings have to be instituted against this person, and this is then done before a special body and that is the military disciplinary court. It can also be decided to institute criminal proceedings against this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, one of the options is that a person can be brought before a disciplinary court. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counter-intelligence is a very specialist field. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What specialisation did you have that was complementary to the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that one belongs to the security organ in itself means that a person can be specialised, can specialise in counter-intelligence. One could be more or less successful in this work, some people did a good job, some people did a poor job, but you could not say that every security organ was the -- or officer was a top specialist in the job. There were precious few such people in our service, and I think that the same applies to the services of the same kind in other states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question, I hope, in a different way. What was it about your specialty that made it beneficial for you to join the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade? What did you add?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm able to understand your question better. When I joined the Guards Brigade, I had already been doing -- performing my tasks as an independent officer in the 317 Signals Regiment in Bijeljina. I did my job in three different republics and also I worked in Sarajevo, so this was a very, very complex situation with the unit that had a number of facilities on top of different mountains and hills that were all very sensitive. I also worked in the 17th Corps in Tuzla, and this was the springboard for me and I was able to move to the 1st Department in the security administration. So the security administration decided that I was able to help the security organ in the Guards Brigade as a professional, primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But doing what? One appoints a person to assist for a reason. What was the gap that you filled or what did you do that improved what they already had?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a vacancy for the assistant for counter-intelligence and they didn't have the right person for that. They did not have an assistant for counter-intelligence, they had the chief, they had an assistant for staff security, they had their desk officers but no assistant for counter-intelligence, and that was the principal reason. Another reason was they were now involved in combat, as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what was it that you did when they went into combat over and above that which could be done by the people from the security organ already there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a simple answer. I systematised any information that we received. I gave them a certain form. I drafted them in the form of reports, proper reports, the way they should be, and these were then submitted to our superior security organ. Any correspondence that we exchanged was very formulaic in terms of the proper format. For a report to be dispatched, it must contain several crucial elements, such as what constitutes the threat. Is there a person or entire group behind this threat. Or some third element: What method are they likely to use in posing this threat? And then any measures that we propose to forestall this threat. If we can't take steps ourselves, we are supposed to seek assistance from our superior officer within our own unit or body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So to simplify it, four principal heads: One, threat identification. Would you agree? I understand that's what you are saying. With regard to the Vukovar scenario, would it be right to say that the threat identification principally involved ascertaining such things as Ustasha strength, who was resisting, and the identification of leaders and units? Would that be right? And that's not a complete list; I just do it by way of example.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree on the whole except for numerical strength and enemy units. This is intelligence, strictly speaking, and not counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is causing the threat, if one looks at this in general terms, what was the conclusion, the general conclusion of your reports when it came to what was causing the threat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to word this properly in a number of sentences. I will say the following: We had information to indicate that in the Vukovar area, there had appeared a member from the Ustasha enemy emigration, Srecko Rover from Australia with a group of people. We had information to indicate there was activity underway there being carried out by extremists from the Croatian Party of Rights, the HSP. We had information to indicate that in the Vukovar area, important political and military figures had been arriving, top-level political and military figures from the Republic of Croatia garnering significant support in humanitarian terms, and all these provided sufficient elements, sufficient proof for us to reach the conclusion that we were up against an enemy to be reckoned with who was in fact already carrying out combat operations. And if I may just add this: On our side, in terms of our counter-intelligence activity, wherever you have emigrants appearing who tend to be the worst extremists, politically speaking, and in any other sense, one thing you can always expect is sabotage and acts of terror. If you've been following my testimony closely over the last two days, one of the focuses of our activity, in addition to discovering moles in our own service, foreign agents, was to forestall any extremist action taken by such emigrants present in the area, as Srecko Rover and the HSP units affiliated with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move off this topic fairly soon given the time table, but can I suggest the following to you: That there are two principal consequences, and I don't criticise, I merely draw attention to them. One, that the involvement of what you would call emigres and their involvement could, at that time, have had consequences for other areas of Croatia where there was conflict. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that if there were things like that happening elsewhere, that was only to be expected, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And secondly, that in the identification of leaders in the Vukovar area, that would facilitate counter-measures to be taken by you. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Counter-measures to protect our units, to familiarise our own units at the front end about what they are up against, to put it in the simplest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You used a phrase yesterday which was translated as "the security organ without informers has no raison d'etre."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Precisely so, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I've used the word "informers," and in actual fact I think you used the word "collaborators"; that was the translation. But I suspect it could be collaborators or informers as almost synonymous. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree, unfortunately. I said a security organ with no collaborators has no raison d'etre. I mean a security organ which creates no collaborators in the true and proper sense of the word, which means someone who has gone through the full set of training measures in order to be enlisted, so to speak. But any security organ has numerous other sources. This, however, is something official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But can I suggest that the word "collaborator" can have a more general application. That a collaborator, in general terms, could mean a person who is sympathetic to a particular cause and assists that cause in the pursuit of its goal. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is entirely erroneous. A collaborator is a collaborator and no other term can possibly be used. Any other source of information can be called whatever one likes. A collaborator is a collaborator is a collaborator. This is an official relationship between the security organ, on the one hand, and the person they work with. Information about this collaborator is only available to the security organ itself. So that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it is also correct to say that at that time, that you were receiving assistance from individuals within the Vukovar area who were behind the lines of the Croatian forces. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have been very happy, indeed, had that been the case, had we had the possibility. Throughout the entire operation, I never had occasion to receive any information whatsoever from the opposite side. Perhaps the intelligence people did, but we didn't. We, as security officers, in an unknown area, have no time or capability to create a foothold on the other side, as it were. And this was not a single area in a manner of speaking, meaning we were not actually holding that area. We were limited to our own units, to our facilities at Topcider. Once we were in an unknown area, it was only natural that we would start creating our own network ahead of the front end and then down the depth of our units, as they were deployed. I'm not sure if I'm making any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Therefore, if that is the case, if there was evidence of directed artillery or mortar fire on to walls -- on to wells or water Bowsers, that had to be a direct consequence of artillery direction and not collaborator direction within Vukovar. That is correct, then, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I am not an artillery man myself. I am into telecommunications. I don't know about artillery fire, how it is directed, guided, and how targets are hit. You might be right, but I just don't understand your question entirely. So perhaps I'd best phrase my answer in the following terms: I don't know how artillery fire is guided, and I was never the commander of an artillery unit. I was the commander of a signals unit, but it's nothing like an infantry unit, not even in the remotest sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that a member of the security organ -- or as a member of the security organ, you're not in a position to control artillery fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand me. I am entirely unable to have anything to do with artillery. I know nothing about artillery. That is not my field. I think it would constitute a great insult to true artillerymen if I were to take their position and start doing anything about it, firing a cannon and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Or directing fall of shot?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware of, the way an army is organised, only an artillery man can carry out reconnaissance and scout for enemy's positions. Only a person like that knows what to do. So one needs to have an artillery man doing that, or, alternatively, one needs to have someone who is very close to artillery units or the place being targeted, so this person then provides feedback and tells the artillery men that the targets are not being hit. That's as far as I can tell you about guiding artillery fire, but I'm no expert myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I seem to remember that yesterday -- I seem to remember that yesterday you indicated that there was a line for building artillery shells exclusively for Vukovar; is that right? It's an inelegant way of putting it. A production line for the specific purpose of being used in Vukovar. That was your evidence, I believe, yesterday, and I see Mr. Lukic nodding no, but the page number is 15537, 10 down to 17. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what I said yesterday, if indeed that was yesterday. I know I was talking about that. While I worked for the 1st Department of the security administration, my colleagues and I exchanged a lot of information about the fact that equipment and ammunition were being produced for specific purposes as well as shot. And the fact that there were problems about production. They said there was a possibility that any bullets or missiles filled with this sort of shot would be dysfunctional and not quite up to scratch. We had information to indicate that our own artillery were firing at our positions, not the enemy. I remembered that bit of information. And I called for them to provide the serial numbers of all these missiles and ordinants just to make sure that it wasn't us who had received this dysfunctional or defective ammunition. It could have been another unit as well. So that's what I was talking about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that's not what I'm talking about. What I'm talking about is that there was a production line for shells to be used at Vukovar. It was an exclusively production line. That was the suggestion that you made yesterday; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I would like to look at the transcript to see. But I didn't say that there was a production, the specific purpose of which was to be shipped to Vukovar and used there, as specifically by our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will read it out for you. "We received word at the time that there were acts of sabotage in progress." Never mind that. "Shells were being produced in Travnik and in other factories across the country. By the same token, we realised that there was a production line at the time shells being produced with the specific purpose of being used in Vukovar in fighting around Vukovar." So I'm asking you, quite simply, about the production line that you say was specifically for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is normally good, but I don't think I ever said anything like that, that there was a special series of ammunition, special lots being produced for the specific explicit purpose of being used in Vukovar. I'm quite convinced -- maybe that was the interpretation you got, but I'm quite certain that I couldn't possibly have said anything like that. This is simply not true, that something was being specifically produced in order to be used in Vukovar. I know what special production is. I know how that is done. I worked with the security organ later on and I was in touch with those people. It is impossible that I should have said this that special ammunition was being produced in order to be used in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we can check that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can check that. I will move on to another topic. We have heard evidence that the JNA had a listening capability to various forms of communication coming out of Vukovar going elsewhere. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, somebody probably was doing that. The same probably applied to the other side. They probably had a listening capability to use against our own lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just tell us, please, the systems that you had available to you to listen in to conversations. You don't have to go into great detail, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Guards Brigade security organ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the entire command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you tell us either, it won't take you long to inform us. Perhaps I can ask the question in this way. As far as you're aware, the JNA at that time had the capability to listen into telephone conversations; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There were special centres for listening in to telephone conversations as well as specialised units for that purpose within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we short-circuit this, it's correct to say that it was -- I don't know if common knowledge would be right, but it was apparent that there was an attempt to broker an agreement for a surrender; do you agree with that? And that was known by the JNA because they were listening to the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be very specific about this. These surveillance centres or electronic surveillance centres monitoring any activity by the enemy, or any activity that we ourselves are carrying out, are not related to counter-intelligence, they are related to intelligence, and these are two very distinct types of services back in our country. It used to be that way at the time and I believe it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the reality is even if you don't know specifically what was being said, you were aware that the capability existed. Would that be the summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. You have told us, moving on to a different topic again, that there was a form of government in existence at the time of the fall of Vukovar. Perhaps not government, but form of administration. Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my evidence. All I said was there was a police station in Negoslavci which was part of the civilian authorities that were there. Not a form of government, though. I knew there was such a thing as a Ministry of the Interior and it is a government body. All there was in Negoslavci was a police station. But it is not really a government, it is a police station. It's all that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If that's what your evidence is, I'll ask you no further questions on it. Would Your Honour forgive me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies for moving around from topic to topic but perhaps that's the sort of evidence you have given. We have heard that the word "terrorist" was used on occasion when describing the defenders of Vukovar, the Croatian defenders of Vukovar. Would it be right to say that that was a view taken by certain members of the JNA, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not exactly sure that all members of the JNA defined the enemy like that. However, there's a difference between the regular armed forces of a country and terrorists, legally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean the answer is "yes"? Not necessarily by you, but that was a view expressed by some?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly expressed that view, but you're asking me, so I'm telling you. I could be caught thinking that way about certain emigres that we had ample information on, such as Srecko Rover, yes. As for such armed forces as the ZNG and the MUP, the Croatian forces, they could not have been labelled like that. The essential distinction was the latter were supported by the government and the former were not, in a sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would you accept from me that there was almost a subcategory of individuals who could be described as "terrorists/criminals"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a sense, yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I then move on to another topic, please. It is this: You were there to systemise the reporting procedure, you have told us that. It's right to say, however, that you yourself signed, I think, a document once and got told off for it, and thereafter and probably before as well, every such document that you created had to be signed by the head of the security organ, is that right, Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Because I could have signed any document but I could not have sealed -- placed a seal on it. I had the authority to sign it if he was prevented from doing that, but in order to keep our reporting proper, we did all we could to ensure that all our reports were signed by the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the purpose of that, I would suggest, is perfectly clear, because by that, it ensured that the chief of the security organ was aware of the content of the document being sent. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Major Sljivancanin is a thorough and was a thorough officer and ensured that before he signed a document, he was aware of its content. That is also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You informed us that Major Sljivancanin, the way you described it, again, I work from my own private notes, you said as follows, and believe me, I'm not trying to catch you out: "When I arrived in the brigade, I knew no one so it was logical for me to stay," I presume by that meaning the command post, "and natural for Sljivancanin to do the rounds for our analysis and reports." Now, that is my brief note. Do you agree with that as a summary of what you said in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you explain to me or perhaps the Court why it was beneficial for him to do the rounds for analysis and reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, counter-intelligence work, when one is in the barracks, is quite different from counter-intelligence work in combat operations. The people that we call our collaborators, this is an official kind of relationship, they know in advance when they have to call in, but because of the combat, the fighting, enemy fire, because it is impossible for them to get some form of transportation, these circumstances forced us to select the person who is really familiar with the unit who had been there right from the start to go around gathering information from these people, because he knew those people. And from all the other people at the forward end to collect the information that would be necessary for our assessment, analysis, and reports. And that is why there was this arrangement. Because 99 per cent of the personnel in the Guards Brigade didn't know me. Maybe even -- the percentage may have been even greater. Some people may have heard of me but that was not enough. And if I were to show up, they would not know who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in simple terms, people will talk more readily and an officer will be able to assess more accurately if the officer is known to the troops and the troops is known to the officer. That is correct, I think, isn't it? That's what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just trying to tell you what situation I would find myself in, because if nobody knows me in a unit and I come there and I say this is who I am, I introduce myself, at the forward end, I don't think that it would be really very good for me. After all, anyone could go there and say I am Sljivancanin's assistant without Sljivancanin being there and they would not know me because I had only just arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect we agree, but maybe it's the way I've put the question. What you are saying is this: Mr. Sljivancanin was known to the troops. Therefore, they would recognise him and speak to him more easily than someone they did not recognise. Do you agree with that? Just as point one.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's only natural, it's easier for you to talk to somebody you know than somebody you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And secondly, that Mr. Sljivancanin had a knowledge of those troops, and therefore he was in a better position to analyse their morale, their state of confidence and problems better than someone like yourself who had just arrived. Would you agree with that as proposition two?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the part of your statement when you say that he knew them better than I did. But nobody could know the actual situation in the unit better than the commander of this unit. Because he is the most responsible person for the morale and the combat readiness in the unit. The commander of the platoon, company, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that in any way at all. All I'm simply saying is in the context of Mr. Sljivancanin or yourself, Mr. Sljivancanin is the right choice or - the better phrase - the better choice than yourself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a better choice because he was in a better position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The function of the security organ or one of its functions is to assess morale, combat readiness, and assess any other problems within a unit. Would you accept that as a general proposition but not an exclusive proposition?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the sense that you are trying to present. The assessment of the morale in the unit is done by the command, and after all, we have the organ for morale monitoring the situation, and we were just a part of this system which is called command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to catch you out. Do you understand? I'm putting forward questions to try and clarify certain issues. All right? So I'm not suggesting it is exclusive. I understand there are other units. But this is one of the functions of the security organ, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I am not in the corner at all. I am -- you are not trying to -- or indeed succeeding in catching me out because this is my area. If you try to ask me any questions that had to do with law, you would probably catch me out quite soon. But I really didn't quite understand the question that followed, so if I could ask you to assist me so that I could assist you by answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am quite sure that this is your area of expertise. All I'm trying to do is to ascertain when you have the security organ, the function of the security organ, along with other units, is to try and understand if there are any problems and to try and resolve those problems, whatever they may be.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that this was the case and he would propose some measures to this end and provides a prompt warning to the relevant organs about possible causes and consequences of any activities that might damage the combat readiness and of course attends the analysis of the morale and combat readiness situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is right, is it not, that you were aware that the Guards Motorised Brigade had subordinated to it - indeed OG South had subordinated to it - various TO units. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the order, but I assume that this order existed in light of the fact that the Guards Brigade was renamed by the fact that some other units were attached to it, and then it was called the Operations Group South. This was a task for some temporary formation with different units performing a certain task within a given time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what I am suggesting to you, that one of the tasks that Major Sljivancanin performed was to assess those potential problems not only of regular soldiers from the Guards Motorised Brigade but other units that were subordinated to them at that time. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're completely off the mark. The other units had their own security organs that did or should have done precisely the same thing that we were doing in the Guards Motorised Brigade. So Major Sljivancanin could not have assessed the work being done in the attached formations, to purport to be their chief, to issue their tasks, and I'm now referring to the security organs there, and least of all, to any other organs in those other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what about an assault detachment? Is it not made up of regular and irregular units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of irregular units you are referring to. Perhaps you could be a bit more specific and then I will be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, such members as the TO.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're way off the mark again, Mr. Moore. The TO was part of the armed forces of the SFRY, and the armed forces consisted of the JNA and the TO. So these were two constituent elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, one of the things that has to be taken into account, surely, when you are compiling reports is that there may be lines of demarcation between units, but often trouble from what I will call irregular units can filter in sideways and create difficulties and problems. And anybody going round will often hear that. And that's just a question of common sense, that's not a question of military hierarchy, is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a matter of common sense. But I simply don't know what irregular units you are talking about. If you told me, then I would be able to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the fact of the matter is, you weren't there and you wouldn't be able to answer that question. But all I'm asking is the function of Major Sljivancanin going round, you said, was on a regular basis; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, you could say that. He wasn't simply walking from one soldier to another asking them, Well, what's new? Because counter-intelligence work is much more complicated than that. It's not just asking questions. I mean regular counter-intelligence work is necessary. It has to be done on a 24-hour basis. And all the rest is -- you have other tasks and then you have to hear from the field -- from the people in the field about some specific things been specific time-periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you then accept that the TO is indeed a regular unit, such as the Leva Supoderica and volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are mixing apples and oranges here. The TO has its superior command, that would be the republican TO staff, the zone TO staff, and some other formations. So the Territorial Defence and the JNA were constituent parts of the armed forces of the SFRY, and they had their superior organs within the vertical system of the chain of command that that was the only way it could be done. So the lower-level units of the Territorial Defence reported to the zone Territorial Defence staff and then all the way up to the republican TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, then, what is the name of the chief of the security organ for OG South?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no chief of the security in OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I think it's right to say that you just indicated that the Guards Motorised Brigade became OG South, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you misunderstood me. I said that by attaching some other units, the OG South came into being. I didn't say that this brigade became OG South. So the organisational order of the superior command established the OG South from the Guards Brigade and other units that were either brought in or already were deployed in this area. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just suggest that in actual fact it was Major Sljivancanin who was actually the chief of the security organ for OG South, but you presumably would not accept that under any circumstances. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This interpretation is completely erroneous. The security organ of the OG South did not exist because a number of conditions would have had to be met in order for it to come into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal then, please, with the evening of the 19th of November. You were present, I think, when General Vasiljevic came along with another general, Tumanov; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and General Simeon Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just remind us again where it was you were when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they arrived. I just know when they arrived to our offices. They were in the office of the Guards Brigade security organ in the village of Negoslavci. They arrived sometime after 10.00 p.m. This is when they came to our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you remained in those premises throughout the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's also right to say they're not a particular large premises. That is correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the house is, in fact, rather large, and we had at our disposal three rooms: One room where we worked, one large room where we slept, and a bathroom, and the part of the hall. And some other structures of the logistics organ were stationed in the other rooms in the house, the technicians, it seems to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware that apparently General Vasiljevic had contacted Major Sljivancanin who had informed Major Vukasinovic that Croatian soldiers should be collected in possible exchange for JNA soldiers who had been captured?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about this, this thing that you are now telling me. What you just told me, I did not hear about that. As far as I understood, the only reason why they came was because of Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac, and they did well when they prevented us from recording those interviews for propaganda purposes. And it's a good thing they did, because this would probably -- the fallout from that would probably be much worse than we could have imagined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I am not passing any view on that. It's not my business. But I'm curious about one respect of your evidence which you have given so methodically. Would you tell us, please, about the argument that was between Major Sljivancanin and General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because of this thing that I am telling you. He wanted to do that because he thought it would be really great and he said, Well, you have this man here, and it makes no sense for this man to speak against Tudjman whose closest collaborator he was, and the Croatian policy, and you have him there. This is where he was. And I think that this assessment by General Vasiljevic was quite good, that it would have been madness to do that because a person in a situation -- in such a situation cannot really achieve the effects that we had thought it would be possible, either on the people in Serbia, or on the other side, and we knew that they were watching Serbian TV channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The phrase that we have heard has not just been Vasiljevic dictating orders in a loud voice. The phrase that we have heard is "heated exchange" between Sljivancanin and Vasiljevic. Now, a heated exchange in English means that both parties are raising their voices. In this case, it is a major raising his voice to a general which, I would suggest, is a fairly unusual state of affairs, isn't it, Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was not the way it was. Major Sljivancanin, at that time, and I think it is still the case, speaks in a loud and clear voice. To some people, it may look as if it was a quarrel. And if you see somebody moving their hands, the gesticulation, it may appear as an argument. But it was not my impression when those two officers arrived that they were angry with us, that we had done something wrong, apart from this thing that they suggested that it would be bad to do this, and once they explained to us, we saw their points. And after all they did have -- they were senior officers with more experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Major Sljivancanin has a loud and distinctive voice?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the exchange, the heated exchange, your analysis, would that be based on a person who is unfamiliar with Major Sljivancanin's tone and tenor? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you keep referring to this as a heated debate that was supposed to frighten everyone around them. This is not the way I saw it and this was not something that I paid any attention to, to be quite honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you are not the only person who has given evidence in this court. And all I'm simply suggesting to you is this: Often, and this is a question of common sense, I would suggest, often if you hear a person whom you do not know speaking in a loud voice, perhaps one can come to the conclusion that person is yelling or shouting. However, if that person is known to you, to speak in that particular way, then you understand that is quite normal. Do you follow me so far? Da?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand you completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore, what I'm suggesting to you that the phrase "heated exchange" was used by a person who knew Major Sljivancanin probably better than you did. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I follow you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this line of questioning calls for the speculation on the part of the witness but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may prove right but it's too early to decide. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it's not the most withering point, but could I just have an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there may be people who know him better than I do and that that's the impression that they got. I'm sure that many people knew him better than I did. In fact, that holds true for all the members of the security organ in the Guards Brigade, and it's possible that they reached that conclusion. I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to another topic. The evening of the 19th, you say that you remained in the hall -- sorry, you remained in the building. Now, would it be fair to say that a security organ was a small unit and a close unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's a problem to answer this one. If you consider the numerical strength of a regiment or a division, yes, it's small in comparison, of course. But the only thing that a security organ is about is its professionalism. There is no cowtowing, there is no favouritism, no such things as might occur in a different kind of unit. We were, after all, hand-picked to those positions. Special selection methods were used and the selection process took some time. It wasn't about camaraderie. Of course there was friendship, but each relationship within the security organ was strictly professional because that is the only guarantee of survival in that particular line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So on the night of the 19th, morning of the 20th, you slept together with Major Sljivancanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, same room. The security organ room in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be frivolous in any way, please understand that, or suggestive. Did you all have your own beds or did you tend to share beds?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those weren't beds to begin with, just mattresses strewn over the floor. A bed normally takes up more space and we had mattresses lined up, and that's how we slept, military mattresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that on the night of the 19th, the morning of the 20th, I'll call it now the night of the 19th, that you were extremely tired?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. Some people were, some people weren't. If you're asking me, I can't quite claim that I was particularly tired. I hadn't been plowing the field that day, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do see what you mean, but I seem to remember either in your evidence or your proofing note that you indicated that when you saw Major Sljivancanin for the second time at the hospital, you indicated that you were very tired, that when you went to Sremska Mitrovica you would like to go home, and it was for fatigue that you were asking to go home. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would never agree with that. I'm absolutely certain that I never said any such thing, not here or before any of your colleagues. On account of fatigue, no, never. Maybe it was interpreted that way, but I think there should be an audio recording in Serbian somewhere and we can cross-reference the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something. I mentioned the word "fatigue" just once when I spoke about the meetings that we held on a regular basis. Sometimes they weren't that regular, as they say. Because of assignments elsewhere, or because of fatigue in the evening and then it would be postponed for the following morning, and that was the only reference I ever made to the concept of fatigue. But there is no possibility, there is zero possibility of me having used the word "fatigue" in any other constellation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were asked a question when you came to see the Office of the Prosecutor representative, and you said the following, and it was in relation to the night of the 20th when you were at Negoslavci and you allegedly were taking back Dr. Bosanac et al. to Mitrovica. You said as follows: "Late at night I took them to Mitrovica and I had asked Sljivancanin if I could go home for a couple of days as I was tired." Now, it's a very simple point, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would dearly love to hear the original. When I asked to go to Bijeljina, I made no reference at all to being tired, it was about seeing my family after so long. So that's what it was about. I don't believe I ever used the word "fatigue" or "tired." I would love to have that replayed so that I can see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can have that done and Mr. Lukic and I can come to some form of arrangement so let's not concern ourselves on that. Can I also suggest that you described Vujic in that interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the sort of technical problem that occurs when we don't have a transcript. Every time we had a witness in the courtroom and every time they were shown parts of their own testimony they were given a chance to read for themselves. There is an audio recording and we might as well try to play it right away and not leave things for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Technically not feasible, Mr. Lukic. Carry on, Mr. Moore. My light is on. Carry on. Be aware of my light. It's signalling you are about out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Well, I'm nearly finished. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I also suggest in that particular interview that you did describe Mr. Vujic as: "We met a bald, fat, arrogant man whom I later learned was Vujic along the way." All right? So you know exactly that I'm not just making it up. Can I just deal with one or two other matters, while the light is still on.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. No, no, no, no. Not like that. If there's one thing I learned in life, it was to speak cautiously and act cautiously. I'm telling you, and I'm repeating for your benefit something that I said to your investigators. I found that man striking because his approach was haughty somehow, arrogant. He was bald. But I never referred to him as being fat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just move on then, please, because we have got certain time problems. I'm going to suggest to you quite clearly this: That you in no way were able to assess whether Major Sljivancanin was or was not around that location through the early hours of the morning and that what you say is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What location are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the location where you say that in actual fact Mr. Sljivancanin was there all the time and didn't go in and out. Do you remember the point from Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, you're skipping, aren't you? I thought we were moving toward the hospital and the vehicles and -- do you mean the hospital and the date? What about the date? You can just give me the date, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm talking about that night, the night of the 19th/20th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. You should have said it like that the first time around. I can tell you with absolute certainty that that night, following our departure, in some formal and informal exchanges, we were in the rooms of the security organ back in Negoslavci, and we rose together the following morning and we were off to our mission, the mission that we had that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just tell us again, please, what you did on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, I was in the rooms or offices of the security organ back in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Mr. Lukic has asked you, because what you were doing is giving a very detailed account of these two days. I'm asking you to assist us: What were you doing on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I was going about my regular activities in the office of the security organ. Counter-intelligence is not like using a chain saw to split something in two exactly. I didn't go anywhere on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic asked you the question and you had difficulty yesterday. Why is it now you're suddenly remembering?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What difficulty? What exactly do you mean by asking me this? Oh, all right. All right. I remember. He asked me differently. He asked me a different question from the one you're asking. Do I remember something along these lines? Do I remember anything happening on the 18th? So I was surprised. Why was he trying to tie me down to me doing something on the 18th and then he jogged my memory about the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion, so I know full well now why you are phrasing your question the way you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The answer is very simple, Mr. Karan, isn't it? Until Mr. Lukic jogged your memory about the Mitnica Battalion, you couldn't remember what you were even doing on a complete day. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very specific, Mr. Moore, wasn't I? I was not involved in the negotiations or indeed the surrender of that unit. I was doing my own job. So that's why I paused there for a moment trying to remember what it could possibly have been about any actions that I took that might have had to do with the 18th. I wasn't thinking about other bodies from the command or from the security organ. I was just thinking about myself, my own job, because that's how the question was originally phrased. Did I have any reason to specifically remember the 18th? Therefore, I do agree that you certainly noticed a pause in my thinking there but this is the reason. I was thinking about what I did, not what other people were doing. Because we'd spent the whole time discussing my activity, not someone else's activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I be allowed to ask one question and then put my case? May I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're cutting Mr. Lukic down to next to nothing, Mr. Moore. The tape runs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course, the tape. May I ask this question and then I will put my case and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Isn't it right that you have told others that you were doing something specifically on the 18th. Weren't you outlining questions that were to be asked and posed for people who were arrested? Does that jog your memory a little now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. This does nothing to jog my memory. I never said that this is what I had done on that day. That was a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest that unfortunately you have come to give evidence on behalf of --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you have come to assist your colleagues, that with regard to Dr. Bosanac and money, there was no money for the Crisis Staff that they kept looking at. I'd suggest in actual fact there were lists and there were targeted people. I would suggest that you were aware of colleagues of the security organ being present on the night of the 20th and going to Ovcara and that in actual fact you have deliberately come to give evidence to ensure that these -- or this particular defendant has a chance of acquittal. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me a whole lot of different questions. But one thing I'd like to tell you is as far as this money is concerned, my signature was published in all the media, all the printed media in Serbia because I was the president of the commission for this money that we handed over to the security administration. And this was the apparent cause of a quarrel later on between General Vasiljevic and Major Sljivancanin. So none of this is true. I could take a whole lot of time answering your questions, but I think your theory is entirely random, entirely arbitrary. I came here to testify of my own free will. When there is a special task, I will stand up and be counted. I will do it. I will get the job done. I am an honourable person. If there's one thing I hate most of all human qualities, it's lies, and if that were the case indeed, I'd end up truly hating myself. The reason I'm here is to provide details concerning my own work, my own involvement, and the detail of any events that I witnessed. I'm not afraid of anything. I stand by every single word that I have uttered. I have two children. My two children must have a future. You've listed a whole lot of things there that are quite erroneous. I have no recorded interpretation in Serbian. I can't remember everything that you said, but it is entirely frivolous, arbitrary and, above all, entirely erroneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Now, Mr. Lukic, we have at the moment no more than five minutes left on the tape. The courses are obvious. Either you can do what you need in that five minutes or we continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, previously I talked to Mr. Moore. He said he would take about one hour, right, that's impossible to predict. One thing is certain, I can't finish in five minutes. Unfortunately, we may have to meet again tomorrow, 9.00. I think I might take perhaps half an hour, up to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow, Mr. Lukic, at 10.00, rather than 9.00, and I would expect that in one session your questioning will be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Just to keep the tape from running out, I can inform you tomorrow about the next witness and why it is that we have decided to drop the next witness, having confirmed with him and all the relevant topics. But I think we'd best just tell you tomorrow, once we've concluded our redirect of Mr. Karan. And then on Thursday, we start Mr. Vuga. Some exceptional circumstances have intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you meant Tuesday, not Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, must be an interpretation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I once again apologise that the needs of the other Chamber have caused us to reach this difficulty tonight. We resume at 10.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of December, 2006, at 10.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.35 p.m.,
